newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola army offensive causes deaths and injuries.
newsitem.headline: Angola army offensive causes deaths and injuries.

text.p: An Angolan army offensive in the north-eastern Lunda Norte Province still dominated by the former UNITA rebels has caused deaths and injuries, a United Nations official said on Saturday. UNITA said at least 13 people had been killed.
"There are wounded FAA (Angolan army) at Andrada and at Dundo hospitals," said the U.N. official, referring to two Angolan towns along the Zairean border.
"We have also been told that FAA dead have been brought to Dundo."

The Luanda government insists that the operation is against border incursions by armed refugees and not against UNITA, which entered a power-sharing agreement with the government on April 11 that formally ended two decades of civil war which started at independence from Portugal in 1975.
But military sources here say the army offensive, which started on Monday, is aimed at taking back diamond-rich areas in the province controlled by the former rebel movement.

UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, still controls vast areas of the countryside -- some estimates are as high as 70 percent -- including most of the diamond-producing areas.

On Friday Isaias Samakuva, UNITA's top representative to the Joint Commission, the body overseeing Angola's peace process, told Reuters that at least 13 people had been killed at the town of Buya in Lunda Norte by government artillery fire.
His deputy Brigadier General David Horacio said a series of towns had fallen to government control in the past few days in Lunda Norte and that the FAA was moving to the west.
The Angolan army has been unavailable for comment but Angola's Minister of Territorial Administration, Faustino Muteka, told the Luanda daily Jornal de Angola there was no offensive under way.
The borders were being protected against military incursions from Zaire, he said. "We are only trying to protect the border."

The Angolan government began tightening control of its borders after an estimated 17,000 Rwandan refugees arrived at the Dundo crossing in April and more recently the reported entry into Angola of 25,000 refugees.

Several reports, including one by an Angolan minister, say many refugees are armed. Other officials claim members of the former Rwandan Hutu-led army and their allies, who are largely blamed for their country's 1994 genocide, are among them.
UNITA officials in Luanda say the government is using the refugees as an excuse to go into the UNITA areas.

An official close to the peace process here said the chief of the U.N.'s 6,000-plus peace-keeping operation, Alioune Blondin Beye, had met Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos late this week and asked that the military operation be stopped.
"Beye is worried that this is very dangerous to the peace process," said the official.
"He asked dos Santos to stop it, that it could derail the peace process. But dos Santos told him it was a clean-up operation aimed at the armed refugees in the area and had nothing to do with UNITA."
